teaser: A goddess is losing an argument, and Titian stops the clock one step before the door closes.
review_notes:
Year given as 1555; the Met dates its version to the 1550s and scholars discuss workshop participation in the replicas.
Philip II's complaint about a fold in the canvas concerns the Prado version sent to London in 1554, not this canvas.
Titian's letter about showing Venus from the back to vary from the Danae: paraphrased, not quoted.
Raffaello Borghini's 1584 criticism of the departure from Ovid.
Venus's pose derived from the ancient relief known as the Bed of Polyclitus: standard scholarly view, please confirm wording.
Palma Giovane's report that late Titian painted with his fingers.
Cupid awake with a dove is specific to this smaller type of the composition (he sleeps in the Prado version).
The shaft of light at top right is described only as visible; its meaning is not asserted.

lesson.text: His weight is already on the front foot. One hand has the spear up, the other is wound in the leashes of three dogs that want to run. She has thrown both arms around his chest from a seat she is half falling off. In one second he will be gone. Titian paints the second before.

The story comes from the Roman poet Ovid. Venus, goddess of love, falls for a mortal hunter named Adonis. She begs him to stay away from dangerous animals. He goes hunting anyway, and a wild boar kills him that same day. Everyone who saw this painting in the 1550s knew how it ended.
So Titian had no need to show blood or a boar. He could tell the whole tragedy with two bodies pulling in opposite directions. Follow how each one argues without a word.

lesson.title: An argument in three parts
lesson.text: Two people, one decision. Tap to read it piece by piece.

spots.title: Her twisted back
spots.text: Venus turns away from us and screws her whole spine around to hold him. Hips face one way, shoulders another. The pose is uncomfortable on purpose: she had no time to stand up.

spots.title: Two faces
spots.text: He looks down at her, calm, almost amused. We see only a sliver of her profile, tilted up. A young man sure of himself, and a goddess who cannot make him listen.

spots.title: The leashes
spots.text: His lowered hand grips the cords of the hounds. They are taut. The dogs are already pulling him out of the picture, to the right, toward the hunt.

lesson.text: A goddess of beauty shown from behind was a bold choice, and a deliberate one. Titian had just sent the Spanish prince Philip a nude seen from the front. In a letter he explained that this time he wanted to show the other side, so that the room where the pictures hung would be more pleasing to look at.

Philip, the future king of Spain, received his version of this composition in London in 1554, where he had just married the English queen Mary Tudor. He liked it, but complained that the canvas had arrived with an ugly fold across it.

Here is the surprise: this scene is not in Ovid. In the poem, Venus gives her warning and flies off in her chariot, and Adonis ignores it later. Titian invented the embrace and the man tearing himself free. A critic scolded him for it thirty years on. Painters copied it for a century.
Why does the invention work so well? Because the picture is built like a tug of war, and you can trace the rope.
Three lines hold the drama together.

lines.label: Her pull
lines.text: From her trailing foot, up along the back, to the arms locked around his ribs. Venus is one long diagonal leaning to hold him in the left half of the canvas.

lines.label: His escape
lines.text: From the hand on the spear, across his shoulders, down the arm, along the leashes to the big hound's head. Everything about Adonis points right, out of the frame.

lines.label: The only link
lines.text: A short glance joins the two lines. It is the one thing still connecting them, and it is about to break.

lesson.text: Nothing in that structure is stable. She has no footing, he is mid stride, the dogs strain. Earlier Renaissance painters loved balance, figures planted like columns. Titian, in his sixties, wanted a picture that feels like it will come apart if you look away.
Titian did not illustrate Ovid's text. He invented the moment the text skips, the instant of parting, and told the whole myth through two bodies pulling apart.

The design was a hit, and Titian's workshop produced several versions for different buyers. They are not identical. In the New York canvas the little god of love, Cupid, is awake and frightened. And his weapons are no longer in his hands.
Love has been disarmed. Where did Cupid's bow and arrows end up?

spots.title: Hung in a tree
spots.text: The quiver full of arrows and the bow dangle from a branch at the far left, tied with a ribbon. Love's weapons are out of reach at the exact moment they are needed.

lesson.text: Venus's corkscrew pose was not drawn from a model in the studio. Titian adapted it from an ancient Roman relief carving that artists of his day knew and copied, then turned cold marble into warm skin.

That skin is made of very little. By this time Titian had dropped crisp outlines. He worked in soft patches of color laid one over another, letting edges blur, so that flesh, fur and cloud seem to breathe the same air. From across a room it snaps into focus.
A younger painter who watched the old Titian at work reported that he finished his pictures more with his fingers than with his brushes, smudging highlights and shadows directly onto the canvas.

spots.title: A rainbow
spots.text: A pale arc of color curves behind Adonis's raised arm. It is easy to miss against the dark trees.

spots.title: Light through cloud
spots.text: In the top right corner, beams of light break through a brown, stormy sky, over the side of the picture Adonis is heading for.

spots.title: Cupid and a dove
spots.text: The child clutches a white dove, the bird of Venus, and looks back over his shoulder at the quarrel. He is the only one who seems afraid.

spots.title: The dog that sees you
spots.text: Head low, mouth open, this hound looks straight out of the canvas. It is the one pair of eyes in the picture that meets yours.

spots.title: The lead hound
spots.text: The largest dog turns its head back toward its master, waiting. A few loose strokes of white make the fur on its neck.

spots.title: Red velvet
spots.text: Venus sits on a crimson cloth thrown over a rock, with white linen sliding off it. The warm red makes her pale skin look even cooler.

spots.title: The leading foot
spots.text: A hunter's boot and sandal, planted forward and brightly lit. This foot carries the whole decision.

lesson.text: Ovid finishes the story with flowers. Venus finds Adonis dying and makes blood-red anemones grow where he fell, blooms that last only a few days. Titian leaves all of that outside the frame. He gives you the last second in which it could still have gone another way, and lets you hold it.

quiz.question: What did Titian change from Ovid's poem?
options: He invented the scene of Adonis pulling away from Venus's embrace
quiz.explanation: In Ovid, Venus warns him and leaves first; the embrace and escape are Titian's invention.

quiz.question: Why did Titian show Venus from behind?
options: To vary from a nude seen from the front that he had already sent Philip
Because the model refused to show her face
quiz.explanation: He wrote that he wanted to show the other side for variety.

quiz.question: Where are Cupid's bow and arrows in this painting?
options: On the ground by the dogs
Hanging from a tree at the left
quiz.explanation: The quiver and bow dangle from a branch, out of reach.

quiz.question: What is Adonis holding in his lowered hand?
quiz.explanation: The taut cords of the dogs pull him toward the hunt.

quiz.question: How did the old Titian reportedly finish his paintings?
options: With his fingers as much as with brushes
By letting his patrons add details
quiz.explanation: A younger painter described him smudging paint with his fingers.

facts.text: The painting shows the boar attacking Adonis.
facts.explanation: The boar never appears; Titian stops just before Adonis leaves for the hunt.

facts.text: Philip of Spain received a version of this composition while he was in London.
facts.explanation: It reached him there in 1554, just after his marriage to Mary Tudor.

facts.text: One of the dogs looks directly out at the viewer.
facts.explanation: The hound with its head low and mouth open meets your eyes.
